# title: "Let me count the ways to decompose a contingency table"
title: "A large-scale comparison of cross-situational word learning models"
bibliography: refs.bib
csl: apa6.csl
document-params: "10pt, letterpaper"

author-information: > 
    \author{{\large \bf George Kachergis (kachergis@stanford.edu)} \and {\large \bf Michael C.~Frank (mcfrank@stanford.edu)} \\ Department of Psychology, 450 Jane Stanford Way \\ Stanford, CA 94305 USA}

abstract: >
    One problem language learners face is extracting word meanings from 
    scenes with many possible referents. Despite the ambiguity of individual   
    situations, a large body of empirical work shows that people are
    able to learn cross-situationally when a word occurs in different 
    situations. Many computational models of cross-situational word learning   
    have been proposed, yet there is little consensus on the main mechanisms 
    supporting learning, in part due to the profusion of disparate studies and models,
    and lack of systematic model comparisons across a wide range of studies. 
    This study compares the performance of several extant models on a dataset 
    of 44 experimental conditions and a total of 1,696 participants.
    Using cross-validation, we fit multiple models representing theories of both
    associative learning and hypothesis-testing theories of word learning, find two  
    best-fitting models, and discuss issues of model and mechanism identifiability. 
    Finally, we test the models' ability to generalize to additional
    experiments, including developmental data. 
    
keywords: >
    cross-situational word learning; model comparison; language learning

# Introduction

Learning word meanings is a crucial aspect of the process of language acquisition. 
If a learner's task is to connect the words they hear to the potential referents and eventually to generalizable meanings, the challenge appears formidable [@Quine1960]: words are heard in rich and cluttered contexts. 
Yet children learn words very quickly. How do they do this? 

An array of social [@yurovsky2017beyond], pragmatic [@Clark1987; @Markman1992], and linguistic [@Gleitman1990] cues are often available to reduce a learner's uncertainty. 
Yet at its heart, these information sources can be seen as reducing the uncertainty inherent in the task of *cross-situational mapping* [@Frank2009]: that is, cross-referencing which referents a word has consistently appeared with across multiple uses [@Gleitman1990; @Carey1978]. 
If learners can learn cross-situationally, they might be able to pool information about reference (and hence word meaning) over time and learn even absent perfectly disambiguated input in any particular situation. 
Can children (or even adults) learn in this way? 

The general idea of cross-situational word learning has been adopted into a variety of experimental paradigms for testing the word learning ability of infants [e.g., @Smith2008vg; @Vlach2013], children [e.g., @Akhtar1999; @Suanda2014; @Vlach2012eq], and adults [e.g., @Yu2007; @Smith2010th].
In such experiments, participants are typically presented with a series of training trials composed of multiple possible referents (e.g., an array of 2-4 novel objects) and one or more spoken nonce words, and (when possible) instructed to learn the meaning(s) of the presented words.
These training trials typically present 10--20 distinct word-referent pairs to be learned across 10--50 trials, presenting each word/referent 3--10 times across a total span of $<10$ minutes.
Learning is then typically assessed by presenting each word and asking learners to make a forced choice of the best referent, either from the entire set or from a small subset of referents.

People of all ages are able to learn word-object mappings in such paradigms at a level significantly above chance, but their performance is typically far from perfect in all but the most trivial versions of the task [@yurovsky2017beyond].
To test the robustness of such learning, many studies have manipulated training and studied resulting performance.
How often mappings are presented [@Suanda2012; @Kachergis2016], the interval between appearances of a mapping [@Vlach2012eq; @Vlach2013], and the number of mappings presented per trial [@Yu2008] all have been shown to affect learning performance.
In sum, the evidence is strong that people can learn word cross-situationally: we are somehow able to integrate evidence (co-occurrence of words and objects) across trials and use that evidence to learn and remember new word meanings in cross-situational learning experiments.
But what are the psychological mechanisms supporting this process? 
And critically, do these mechanisms support naturalistic word learning?

Computational models provide one strategy for instantiating proposals about mechanism. 
Such models can then be applied to naturalistic data to make a first assessment of whether cross-situational learning could be a viable strategy for word learning "in the wild". 
Accordingly, there has been great interest in creating and testing computational models of this task. 
These models often represent distinct intuitions of how learning operates.
At one extreme, *logical* accounts treat the learner as ruling out meanings that are logically inconsistent with the input [e.g., @Siskind1996].
*Hypothesis-testing* accounts propose that learners entertain a single conjectured referent for a word and revise it only when it is disconfirmed on a later encounter, storing little or nothing about the alternatives [@Medina2011; @Trueswell2013].
*Associative* accounts instead assume learners accumulate graded word-referent strengths across trials, whether by simple co-occurrence tallying, competitive normalization [@Fazly2010], attention weighted by familiarity and uncertainty [@Kachergis2012gi], or prediction-error-driven updating in the tradition of @Rescorla1972.
Related *reinforcement-learning* accounts recast the problem as learning the value of choosing a referent for a word from a reward signal (here, whether the chosen referent is present), bridging the propose-and-verify logic of hypothesis testing with graded, error-driven value updates.
A further question within the associative family is whether the learning rate is fixed or adapts to the learner's current uncertainty, either item-by-item -- as in a Kalman-filter formulation of associative learning [@Dayan2001; @Kruschke2008; @Gershman2015] -- or at the level of the whole system, with learners more alert on trials containing more uncertain items [@Fitneva2017].
<!-- Extant cross-situational word learning models are too numerous to review exhaustively here.  -->

It is unknown which of these models -- or even which broad class of models -- best fits the breadth of experimental data.
While most models of cross-situational learning have typically been tested against at least a few datasets, to our knowledge there has been no systematic comparison of models across a wide variety of experimental conditions.
Identifying the model(s) that best predict human performance is thus an important goal for consolidating this broad literature.
More broadly, identifying such models could be an important step in assessing the contribution of cross-situational learning to word learning more generally.

A separate concern is that the experiments these models are usually evaluated on are small, tightly controlled, and drawn from a narrow population.
A typical adult study presents on the order of a dozen unambiguously referential nonce words, each repeated a handful of times, to English-speaking undergraduates over a few minutes.
Naturalistic input looks very different: word-referent co-occurrences in parent-child interaction are sparse, noisy, massively unbalanced in frequency, and only sometimes about anything present in the immediate scene [@Frank2009; @Medina2011].
A model that captures the fine structure of laboratory performance need not recover word meanings from corpus data, and vice versa.
We therefore also ask how the same models fare when run on transcribed parent-child interaction and scored against a gold-standard lexicon, both at their laboratory-fitted parameters and when re-fit to the corpora.


Thus, the goal of our current study is to test the ability of a range of cross-situational word learning models in accounting for a wide range of experimental data.
Our goal is to scale up both the number of models evaluated and the number of experiment designs (and participants) being used for evaluation.
Different models often contain a range of parameters that must be fit to data, an issue that has hindered previous comparison work, either because the parameters have been allowed to vary freely across multiple conditions, or because model performance is compared on different datasets.
Thus, we focus on out-of-sample prediction of human data using cross-validated parameter fits.
We then examine how well models fit with those parameters generalize to further experiments held out of fitting, including developmental data, and how the models perform on naturalistic parent-child corpora.
All of the models, datasets, and fitting procedures are released as an open-source R package, \texttt{XSLmodels}, so that the comparison can be extended and reproduced.
<!-- Finally, we will interpret the results, and what they entail for theories of cross-situational word learning. -->

# Method

## Procedure

Our goal is to fit a set of models to a set of datasets; members of each of these sets are listed below.
Each model is typically defined as a function that takes input data and a group of parameter values (often between 2--4) and then can be evaluated on test trials (typically multi-alternative forced choice test). 
Each model then returns predictions on each test trial, which can be scored against the "correct" (intended by the design) answer and averaged to produce an analogue to human performance. 
Our primary outcome measure is the correlation between each model's performance for each item in a specific experimental condition and item-level human performance on that same experimental condition. 

Although input data and test trials are features of specific experimental tests, each model has parameters that must be specified. 
Typically the settings of these parameters are critical to the predictive performance of the model. 
Hence, to ensure a fair comparison between models, these parameters must be fit to data. 
In all cases, we optimize parameter values to minimize the sum of squared error (SSE) between model and human performance, weighting the contribution of each condition's SSE by the number of participants in that condition.
We optimize parameters using differential evolution via the DEoptim R package [@DEoptim].
For the stochastic models, each parameter setting was evaluated using a simulated sample of 200 learners.

We conducted two evaluations of models. 
First, we optimize each model's parameters on 80% of data and evaluate on the remaining 20% (5-fold cross-validation).
Second, in the *group fit* regime, we fit each model to all conditions and datasets and evaluate across all data.
Though slightly overfit, this evaluation allows us to make the best test of generalization to other experiments from the literature.

All models, datasets, and fitting procedures are implemented in the open-source R package \texttt{XSLmodels}[^pkg], and every fit reported here was produced with version 0.4.0 of that package.
Porting the models from the research code behind an earlier conference report of this comparison <!-- ToDo (revision): cite the CogSci 2024 proceedings paper once it's in refs.bib --> surfaced several implementation errors, which we corrected, so some results here differ from that report.
Most consequentially, the routine shared by the familiarity- and uncertainty-biased family for seeding initial associations to newly familiar words and objects placed those values in the wrong cells whenever some object had not yet been seen; this affected FU and all of its variants.
In addition, the guess-and-test model never discarded a hypothesis once formed (its disconfirmation step was unreachable), the probabilistic associative model's test-time accuracy was not normalized over referents, and the Bayesian decay model's choice rule normalized over words rather than over referents.
When several words on one trial need new hypotheses at once, the propose-but-verify model now draws each word's proposal independently from the referents present, whereas the earlier implementation drew distinct referents for them.
Finally, we gave every variant of the FU model the same bounds on the parameters they share with FU ($\chi$, $\lambda$, $\alpha$), so that differences among the variants reflect their mechanisms rather than their search ranges.

[^pkg]: \url{https://github.com/kachergis/XSLmodels}; the exact package version used for the fits is recorded with the analysis code.


## Models


We fit nineteen models together with a zero-parameter baseline co-occurrence model.
The original evaluation included the baseline, six associative models (the probabilistic associative model, the familiarity- and uncertainty-biased model, its strength-, uncertainty-, and novelty-biased reductions, a Bayesian decay model, and a Rescorla-Wagner model), two hypothesis-testing models, and two hybrid models that store multiple graded hypotheses for only a subset of the possible associations.
We later added eight more: four variants of the familiarity- and uncertainty-biased model (making its learning rate depend on uncertainty at the trial or item level, giving familiarity a free exponent, or adding learning by elimination), a Kalman-filter generalization of the Rescorla-Wagner model, the reinforcement-and-inference model of @Tilles2013, a reinforcement-learning model, and an episodic memory model (MINERVA 2).
All models and their free parameters are briefly described below.
<!-- ToDo (revision): add a summary table (model x class x #params x key mechanism). -->



### Baseline Co-occurrence Model
The baseline model simply tallies the co-occurrences of any words and objects appearing together on each trial, accumulating the counts in a word $\times$ object matrix $M$.
At test, for word $w_1$ this model selects the correct referent $o_1$ according to @Luce1959 choice from the co-occurrences of $w_1$ with all referents: $P(o_1|w_1) = M_{w_1,o_1} / \sum{M_{w_1,\cdot}}$.
The model's probability of correctly choosing each word per condition is scored against people's average probability of choosing the correct item.
<!-- tried adding a softmax parameter but it didn't help --> 


### Probabilistic Associative Model (PA)
The probabilistic associative model [@Fazly2010] represents the meaning of each word *w* as a probability distribution $p(\cdot | w)$ over the objects appearing across the trials, and incrementally learns these distributions trial-by-trial.
The association between a given *w* and *o* grows more quickly if $p(w|o)$ is already high (a familiarity bias), unless some other word has a strong association with *o*; thus, associations are competitive.
The parameter $\lambda$ is a small smoothing constant added to both the numerator and denominator of each $p(w|o)$, further adjusted in the denominator by a $\beta$ parameter representing the upper bound on the number of symbol types.
At test, the correct referent for each word *w* is chosen according to @Luce1959 choice from the probability distribution over the objects that appeared with that word $p(\cdot | w)$.[^1]

[^1]: The original model implemented a $\theta$-thresholded lexicon that discretized the probability matrix, but we found that including this mechanism resulted in a worse fit to the data.


### Familiarity- and Uncertainty-biased Model (FU)
The familiarity- and uncertainty-biased associative model [@Kachergis2012gi] assumes that learners associate all presented words with all visible objects to some extent, but that they selectively attend more to some of the presented word-object pairings.
Specifically, greater attention is directed to pairings that have previously co-occurred (a familiarity bias), but is also directed to stimuli that have no strong associates, tracked via the entropy (*H*) of their association strengths (e.g., novel stimuli, or stimuli that have diffuse associations with several stimuli). 
Thus, the model grows its association matrix as it experiences each trial, dynamically apportioning a fixed amount of associative weight (learning rate $\chi$) among the possible word-object associations, with the relative weight of the familiarity bias and the uncertainty bias determined by parameter $\lambda$.
Association strengths decay at a rate controlled by parameter $\alpha$.
The update rule for adjusting the association $M_{w,o}$ between a given word $w$ and object $o$ on a given trial is:

\begin{equation}
M_{w,o} =  \alpha M_{w,o} + \frac{ \chi \cdot e^{ \lambda \cdot (H(w) + H(o)) } \cdot M_{w,o}  }{  \sum_{w\in W} \sum_{o\in O} e^{ \lambda \cdot (H(w) + H(o)) } \cdot M_{w,o} }
\label{eq:fullmodel}
\end{equation}

At test, given word $w$ learners use Luce choice, choosing referent $o$ from the \textit{m} given alternatives in proportion to associative strength $M_{w,o}$. 

We also fit a *stochastic sampling* (**FUs**) version of this model [see @Kachergis2017], which uses the same update equation, but samples only a single presented object for each word on a trial instead of updating all possible associations. 
This FU sampling model can still build multiple graded associations for each word (or object), but on any given run will accumulate only a sparse, randomized version of what the full associative model would build.


### Strength-, Uncertainty-, & Novelty-biased (Str,Unc,Nov) Models
We also test three variations of the FU model that use only a subset of the mechanisms of the full model in order to understand the contributions of each mechanism.
The *strength model* lacks the uncertainty bias term, and thus only implements a bias for familiar (i.e., already-strong) associations, with learning rate ($\chi$) and decay ($\alpha$) parameters.

The *uncertainty model* lacks the strength bias term, and thus only implements a bias for stimuli with uncertain (high-entropy) associations.
The *novelty model* also lacks the strength bias term, and substitutes novelty for the entropy terms (e.g., 1/(frequency(*w*)+1) instead of $H(w)$).
These models have all three parameters of the original FU model, and operate in the same way as that model at test. <!--, although $\chi$ and $\beta$ likely trade off.-->


### Bayesian Decay Model (BD)
This previously-unpublished model updates the $p(w|o)$ and the joint probability $p(w,o)$ from trial to trial according to a likelihood function that reinforces the association between *w* and *o* when they co-occur (scaled by parameter $\delta$), and penalizes all associations that are not occurring on the trial (scaled by parameter $\alpha$).
Thus, in contrast to other incremental associative learning models considered here (e.g., Fazly and the Kachergis class of models), this model globally updates the entire association matrix on each trial -- both co-occurring pairs and non-co-occurring pairs, and re-normalizes the tracked probabilities at each time step.
At test, this model uses a softmax choice rule with parameter $\tau$ to select the best referent for each word from the presented alternatives. 


### Rescorla-Wagner Model (R-W)
This associative model is inspired by the prediction-error-based learning model of @Rescorla1972. 
Objects on each trial serve as cues to predict which words will be heard.
When a given word is heard, the associations between that word and each object on the trial are scaled at a learning rate $\beta$ in proportion to the magnitude of the difference between the prediction and the maximum association value ($\lambda$). 
Each trial, the association matrix is subject to decay (parameter $\alpha$).
At test, this model uses Luce choice to select the best referent for each word from the presented alternatives.


### Propose-but-Verify Model (PbV)
In the propose-but-verify hypothesis testing model [@Trueswell2013], a presented referent is selected at random for any presented word that has no remembered referent. 
The next time that word occurs, the previously-proposed referent is remembered with probability $\alpha$, a free parameter. 
If the remembered referent is verified to be present, the future probability of recalling the word is increased by parameter $\epsilon$. 
If the remembered referent is not present, the old hypothesis is assumed to be forgotten and a new proposal is selected from the available referents.
When several words on a trial need new proposals at once, each is drawn independently from the referents present, so two words may propose the same referent.


### Guess-and-Test Model (GnT)
The guess-and-test hypothesis testing model is based on the description given by @Medina2011 of a one-shot (i.e. "fast mapping") learning model, which posits that "i) learners hypothesize a single meaning based on their first encounter with a word, ii) learners neither weight nor even store back-up alternative meanings, and iii) on later encounters, learners attempt to retrieve this hypothesis from memory and test it against a new context, updating it only if it is disconfirmed."
<!-- In summary, guess-and-test learners do *not* reach a final hypothesis by comparing multiple episodic memories of prior contexts or multiple semantic hypotheses. -->
We give this model two free parameters: a probability of successful encoding ($s$, hypothesis formation), and a probability $f$ of forgetting a hypothesis at retrieval. 
At test, for each word the model chooses the currently hypothesized referent.
<!-- This model is quite similar to the guess-and-test model formally analyzed by @Blythe2010 to determine the theoretical long-term efficacy of cross-situational word learning. -->


### Pursuit Model (Pur)
The pursuit model [@Stevens2017pursuit] is a hybrid model, potentially storing graded associations involving a given word and multiple referents (or vice-versa), while on any given trial greedily pursuing the  strongest association for each presented word.
If the strongest associated referent for a given word $w$ is present on the trial, the association is strengthened at a rate determined by $\gamma$.
If the strongest referent for $w$ is not present, the association is weakened (scaled down by ($1-\gamma$)) and the association with a random other available referent is strengthened.
Novel words are given an initial association of strength $\gamma$ with the available referent whose strongest association is the smallest, implementing an uncertainty bias in forming associations for novel words.
A given word-object association only enters the lexicon if $p(o|w) > \theta$, a threshold parameter.
At test, this model chooses the best referent for each word by Luce choice from the lexicon, which is not necessarily 1-to-1.


The models below were added after the initial comparison.


### FU with Trial-Level Attention (FU-A)
This variant of the FU model implements the "system-level" attention account of @Fitneva2017, on which learners are more alert -- allocating a higher learning rate -- on trials whose items are more uncertain (for instance early in training, or after many items have been mispaired).
On each trial, the associative weight the FU model distributes (learning rate $\chi$) is additionally scaled by the ratio of that trial's mean object entropy to the mean entropy of all objects seen so far.
The model has the same three free parameters as the FU model ($\chi$, $\lambda$, $\alpha$) and uses the same Luce choice rule at test.


### FU with Item-Level Prediction Error (FU-P)
This variant replaces the FU model's normalization step -- which distributes a fixed total amount of associative weight across the word-object pairings on a trial -- with an item-level, Rescorla-Wagner-style [@Rescorla1972] prediction error term: the amount learned about a given word-object association is scaled by how far the word's predicted strength (summed over the trial's objects) falls short of a maximum value.
Surprising (e.g., initially mispaired) items therefore draw more learning than the normalized model allows.
Because there is no normalization step, associations are kept in their valid range by flooring them at zero and capping them at their maximum value.
The model has the same three free parameters as the FU model and uses Luce choice at test.


### FU with a Familiarity Exponent (FU-G)
In the FU model, the attention a pairing receives on a trial is the product of an uncertainty term, $e^{\lambda (H(w) + H(o))}$, whose influence is set by the free parameter $\lambda$, and the pairing's current strength $M_{w,o}$, which enters linearly with no free weight of its own.
This variant raises the familiarity term to a free power $\gamma$, replacing $M_{w,o}$ with $M_{w,o}^{\gamma}$ in both the numerator and the denominator of Equation \ref{eq:fullmodel}.
Setting $\gamma = 1$ recovers the FU model; $\gamma < 1$ gives diminishing returns to already-strong pairings, dampening the model's "rich get richer" dynamic, while $\gamma > 1$ amplifies it toward winner-take-all.
The model has four free parameters ($\chi$, $\lambda$, $\alpha$, $\gamma$) and uses Luce choice at test.


### FU with Learning by Elimination (FU-E)
This variant adds inference by elimination [cf. @Halberda2003eg] to the FU model's allocation of attention.
If the other words and objects on a trial are already confidently paired with each other, the remaining word and object probably go together, so their pairing should draw attention even while it is still weak; in the FU model, by contrast, already-strong pairs on a trial draw attention *away* from such a pairing.
Each pair $(w', o')$ on the trial has a mutual confidence $q(w', o') = P(o' | w')\,P(w' | o')$, computed from the row- and column-normalized associations, and a pairing $(w, o)$ receives elimination support $s(w, o) = \sum_{w' \neq w,\, o' \neq o} q(w', o')$ -- how much of the rest of the trial is already accounted for.
The share of the trial's associative weight given to $(w, o)$ is then $\big(b(w, o) + \epsilon\, s(w, o)\big) / \big(1 + \epsilon \sum s\big)$, where $b(w, o)$ is the FU model's normalized share, so $\epsilon = 0$ recovers the FU model.
The model has four free parameters ($\chi$, $\lambda$, $\alpha$, $\epsilon$) and uses Luce choice at test.


### Kalman Filter Model (KF)
The Kalman filter model [@Dayan2001; @Kruschke2008; @Gershman2015] generalizes the Rescorla-Wagner model's error-driven update by tracking each word-object association as a Gaussian belief -- a mean strength $\mu_{w,o}$ and a variance $\sigma^2_{w,o}$ representing the learner's uncertainty about it.
On each trial, an association's update toward its target is scaled by that association's *Kalman gain*, $\sigma^2_{w,o} / (\sigma^2_{w,o} + \sigma^2_{obs})$, which makes the effective learning rate adaptive: large while an association is still uncertain and automatically shrinking as evidence accumulates.
Between trials, every association's variance grows by $\tau^2$, so the model can still revise a well-learned belief rather than freezing.
The model has three parameters -- process noise $\tau^2$, observation noise $\sigma^2_{obs}$, and initial uncertainty $\sigma^2_0$ -- of which only two are identifiable (scaling all three by a constant leaves the learned matrix unchanged).
At test, it uses Luce choice over the mean association matrix.
<!-- ToDo (revision): decide whether to fix sigma2_obs and report P = 2 for KF in Table 1; currently all three are fit and P = 3. -->


### Reinforcement-and-Inference Model (TF)
The model of @Tilles2013 [see also @tilles2012minimal] represents each word's meaning as a probability distribution over the objects seen so far, updated by two processes.
*Reinforcement*, with strength $x$, transfers confidence for each word heard on a trial from the objects absent from that trial to those present.
*Inference*, with strength $b$, implements a form of mutual exclusivity: a novel word assigns extra probability to the novel objects present on its first trial, and for familiar words *not* heard on a trial, confidence is transferred away from the objects present toward absent ones.
Both updates are scaled by a word-specific learning efficiency that starts at $\alpha_0$ while the word's distribution is maximally uncertain and rises toward 1 as its entropy falls; the remaining share of each update relaxes the distribution toward uniform, acting as noise.
The model has three free parameters ($x$, $b$, $\alpha_0$) and uses Luce choice over these distributions at test.


### Softmax Reinforcement Learning Model (RL)
The reinforcement learning model recasts word learning as learning, from a reward signal, the value of choosing each referent for a word.
Unlike every other model considered here -- all of which update every word-object pair that co-occurs on a trial -- this model makes a discrete choice: for each word heard, it samples a single candidate referent from a softmax policy over its current values for all known objects (its current best guess at that word's meaning), analogous to the way the propose-but-verify and pursuit models commit to a single hypothesis before checking it.
It then observes whether that referent is present in the scene (reward $= 1$) or not (reward $= 0$) -- the only feedback available in a task with no trial-by-trial correct answer -- and updates only the chosen value by a delta rule, $Q_{w,o} \leftarrow Q_{w,o} + \eta\,(\text{reward} - Q_{w,o})$.
It has two free parameters: the learning rate $\eta$ and a softmax inverse temperature $\beta$ governing how sharply choices favor the highest-valued referent.
At test, the model's probability of choosing the correct referent for a word is read directly from the same softmax policy it learned with.
This model thus shares the propose-and-verify logic of the hypothesis-testing models but replaces their all-or-none keep/discard rules with graded value learning and explicit, tunable exploration.


### MINERVA 2 Episodic Memory Model (M2)
Unlike every other model here, each of which maintains a single word $\times$ object association matrix, MINERVA 2 [@Hintzman1984; @Hintzman1986] stores each training trial as a separate episodic trace.
Words and objects are represented as random feature vectors, and a trial's trace concatenates the sum of its words' vectors with the sum of its objects' vectors; memory is exact, with no decay or forgetting.
At test, a word probe activates every trace in proportion to the cube of its similarity to that trace's word half, and the activation-weighted sum of all traces -- the "echo" -- is compared on its object half with each candidate object.
These similarities are exponentiated by a single free parameter $X$, which sets how sharply choice favors the best-matching object, and normalized as in Luce choice.
The dimensionality of the feature vectors (100) is a fixed representational choice rather than a fitted parameter; because the vectors are random, the model is stochastic.
Two further distributed and episodic memory models, TODAM [@Murdock1982] and REM [@Shiffrin1997], are implemented in \texttt{XSLmodels} but are 20--40 times more expensive to evaluate, which put fitting them at the scale of this comparison out of reach; we leave them to future work.


## Data

```{r load-data}
# The modeled conditions are XSLmodels::xsl_datasets (0.4.0: 56 conditions
# -- the original 44, plus 5 temporal-contiguity conditions from Kachergis,
# Yu & Shiffrin 2009, 3 from Suanda et al. 2014, and 4 from Koehne et al.
# 2013). Every count/range below is computed, not hard-coded.
nConds   <- length(xsl_datasets)
totItems <- sum(sapply(xsl_datasets, \(d) length(d$accuracy)))
totSs    <- sum(sapply(xsl_datasets, \(d) d$n_subj))
nTrials  <- sapply(xsl_datasets, \(d) length(d$train$words))
nPairs   <- sapply(xsl_datasets, \(d) length(unique(unlist(d$train$words))))
wPerTr   <- unlist(lapply(xsl_datasets, \(d) lengths(d$train$words)))
oPerTr   <- unlist(lapply(xsl_datasets, \(d) lengths(d$train$objects)))
rng      <- \(x) paste(range(x), collapse = "--")
```

The modeled data are average accuracies from `r totItems` word-object pairs in `r nConds` experimental conditions, in which a total of `r format(totSs, big.mark=",")` subjects participated.
A table containing details of each condition is available on OSF[^2], along with the full trial orderings and aggregate human performance.
Each condition consists of an ordered list of `r rng(nTrials)` training trials, each presenting `r rng(wPerTr)` words and `r rng(oPerTr)` objects, with a total of `r rng(nPairs)` word-object pairs to be learned per condition.
At test, participants heard each word and were asked to select the best referent from either all $m$ presented objects (*m*-alternative forced choice; AFC), or from a subset (e.g., 4AFC).
The bulk of these data have been previously published: data from 13 of the conditions were reported in @Kachergis2013nat, data from 12 conditions are from @Kachergis2012gi, and data from another nine conditions are from @Kachergis2016.
Data from several conditions were contributed by Chen Yu's lab at Indiana University, and have not been published before.
To these 44 conditions of the original comparison we added five from @Kachergis2009tc, which manipulated the temporal contiguity of repeated word-object pairs; three from @Suanda2014, which varied contextual diversity for 6-year-old children; and four from @Koehne2013, which varied the order in which adults encountered each noun's two differently frequent referents.
The Suanda et al. and Koehne et al. conditions were held-out generalization tests in the earlier report of this comparison, and report only condition-level accuracy, so each of their items is assigned its condition's mean.

[^2]: Information about the dataset: [https://osf.io/REDACTED](https://osf.io/s2aty/?view_only=c91c852f00b847e0a71d5f4deaf7b7a5)

### Naturalistic Corpora

To ask whether any of these models could plausibly learn from the input children actually receive, we also ran them on two transcribed corpora of caregiver speech to young children, bundled with XSLmodels.
The **Rollins corpus** [@Rollins2003] is the CHILDES corpus that @Frank2009's Bayesian model was originally fit to: 619 caregiver utterances to 9-month-olds, 416 word types, 22 co-present object types, and a curated gold-standard lexicon of 34 word-object pairs.
The **FM corpus** [@Frank2013fm] is larger and more naturalistic: 4,763 utterances, 1,122 word types, 30 object types, and a gold lexicon of 41 curated pairs (the corpus also ships stricter and more permissive gold-lexicon variants, not used here).
Unlike the laboratory conditions above, neither corpus has human referent-selection data to compare against; instead, a model's learned word-object matrix is scored against the gold lexicon directly, as the best-threshold F-score over precision and recall (sweeping the matrix threshold that separates a "learned" pairing from noise).
Because a large fraction of caregiver utterances are not about anything in the immediate scene at all, we also ran a Bayesian model built for exactly this setting -- @Frank2009's joint intentional inference over the whole corpus, optionally extended with a Rational Speech Act pragmatic listener [`fgt2009()`/`fgt2009_rsa()`; not part of the trial-by-trial models above, since it has no learning trajectory to compare against per-condition human accuracy].

```{r load-group-fits}
# gfd / group_fits come from paper/load_fits.R, sourced in the libraries chunk

Nitems = nrow(gfd) / length(unique(gfd$Model))
group_fit_tab <- gfd %>% filter(!is.na(HumanPerf)) %>%
  group_by(Model) %>%
  summarise(SSE = sum((ModelPerf-HumanPerf)^2), #/ Nitems,
            r = cor(ModelPerf, HumanPerf)) %>%
  arrange(SSE)
```


```{r load-cv-fits}
# cv_group_fits / cvg come from paper/load_fits.R, sourced in the libraries chunk.
#
# Table 1 metric: the quantity the fits minimize -- each condition's SSE
# (summed over its items), averaged over conditions weighted by n_subj.
#  - CV SSE: every condition scored once, out of fold (at the parameters fit
#    to the other four folds), pooled over all conditions.
#  - Group SSE: recomputed from the group fit's predictions (gfd), NOT
#    DEoptim's reported optimum: for stochastic models that optimum is the
#    minimum over thousands of noisy evaluations and so is biased low (by
#    .007-.033 here); gfd re-simulates at the best parameters (n_sim = 200),
#    an unbiased estimate. For deterministic models the two are identical.
#  - r: item-level correlation of out-of-fold predictions with human accuracy.
wsse_by_model <- function(df) df %>% filter(!is.na(HumanPerf)) %>%
  group_by(Model, condnum) %>%
  summarise(sse = sum((ModelPerf - HumanPerf)^2), n = first(Nsubj), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(Model) %>% summarise(wSSE = sum(sse * n) / sum(n), .groups = "drop")

fold_range <- function(m) {
  f <- cv_group_fits[[m]]$folds
  if (is.null(f)) return(c(NA_real_, NA_real_))   # round-1 fallback has no per-fold record
  range(map_dbl(f, "test_sse"))
}
# the baseline has no parameters (not cross-validated): its out-of-fold
# predictions are its group predictions, scored on each fold's conditions
fold_conds <- map(cv_group_fits[[1]]$folds, "test_conditions")
baseline_fold_sse <- if (length(fold_conds)) map_dbl(fold_conds, \(cc)
  filter(wsse_by_model(filter(gfd, Model == "baseline", condnum %in% cc)), Model == "baseline")$wSSE) else NA

fit_tab <- wsse_by_model(cvg) %>% rename(cv = wSSE) %>%
  left_join(cvg %>% group_by(Model) %>% summarise(r = cor(ModelPerf, HumanPerf)), by = "Model") %>%
  bind_rows(tibble(Model = "baseline",
                   cv = filter(wsse_by_model(gfd), Model == "baseline")$wSSE,
                   r = with(filter(gfd, Model == "baseline"), cor(ModelPerf, HumanPerf)))) %>%
  left_join(wsse_by_model(gfd) %>% rename(group = wSSE), by = "Model") %>%
  mutate(lo = map_dbl(Model, \(m) if (m == "baseline") min(baseline_fold_sse) else fold_range(m)[1]),
         hi = map_dbl(Model, \(m) if (m == "baseline") max(baseline_fold_sse) else fold_range(m)[2])) %>%
  left_join(select(model_meta, Model, abbr, class, P), by = "Model") %>%
  arrange(cv)

# unweighted alternative (SSE summed over items, ignoring sample size), for the text
item_sse <- cvg %>% filter(!is.na(HumanPerf)) %>% group_by(Model) %>%
  summarise(sse = sum((ModelPerf - HumanPerf)^2), .groups = "drop") %>% arrange(sse)
```

```{r table1-text}
fmt3 <- \(x) sub("^0\\.", ".", sprintf("%.3f", x))
listify <- \(x) if (length(x) <= 2) paste(x, collapse = " and ") else paste0(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), ", and ", tail(x, 1))
b_row  <- filter(fit_tab, Model == "baseline")
models <- filter(fit_tab, Model != "baseline")
cv_of  <- \(m) fmt3(fit_tab$cv[match(m, fit_tab$Model)])
TOL <- .01  # "near the baseline": CV SSE within .01 of it
better <- filter(models, cv < b_row$cv - TOL)$abbr
near   <- filter(models, abs(cv - b_row$cv) <= TOL)$abbr
worse  <- filter(models, cv > b_row$cv + TOL)$abbr
item_top <- abbr_of(item_sse$Model[1:2])
```

Table 1 summarizes each model's fit.
Because parameters were fit by minimizing each condition's squared error, weighted by its number of participants, we report that same quantity for the cross-validated (CV) fits -- in which each condition is scored once, at parameters fit without it -- and for the group fit to all `r nConds` conditions.
The best CV fits were from `r models$abbr[1]` (SSE = `r fmt3(models$cv[1])`), `r models$abbr[2]` (`r fmt3(models$cv[2])`), and `r models$abbr[3]` (`r fmt3(models$cv[3])`), whose errors on the five folds' held-out conditions overlap substantially.
<!-- ToDo (revision, D2): add the paired fold / bootstrap-over-conditions comparison of the top tier here. -->
The order within this top group depends on how conditions are weighted: ranking by squared error summed over all `r totItems` items, ignoring sample size, puts `r item_top[1]` first and `r item_top[2]` second.
Compared with the zero-parameter baseline co-occurrence model (CV SSE = `r fmt3(b_row$cv)`, $r$ = `r sub("^0\\.", ".", sprintf("%.2f", b_row$r))`), `r length(better)` models fit better by more than `r TOL` (`r listify(better)`), `r listify(near)` fit within `r TOL` of it, and `r listify(worse)` fit worse.
<!-- ToDo (revision): the next sentence is model-specific -- re-check after any refit that R-W and KF still sit at the parameter bounds where they reduce to counting. -->
The Rescorla-Wagner and Kalman filter models (CV SSE = `r cv_of("rescorla-wagner")` and `r cv_of("kalman_filter")`) are best fit at parameters where learning is so slow relative to the associations' asymptote that each co-occurrence adds a nearly constant increment: at their best, both reduce to tallying co-occurrences.
Correlations between data and models are presented in Figure 1.

## Generalization Experiment Results

```{r gen-exps}
# Generalization results from fits/generalization_with_package.R: each model
# run at its 53-condition group-fit parameters on experiments outside that
# fit. Two tiers: Medina 2011 and Smith & Yu 2008 are genuinely held out;
# Suanda 2014 was held out in the CogSci version but has since been added to
# xsl_datasets, so its numbers here come straight from the group fit
# (tier == "now in fit set").
# NOTE (revision, 2026-09-13): Koehne et al. (2013) is likewise now in
# xsl_datasets/the group fit, but per author feedback it is no longer
# reported as a generalization result at all -- it's just an in-sample
# condition set now (see Table 1), not something to single out here.
load(here("fits/generalization_with_package.RData"))

gen_wide <- gen_exps %>%
  select(model, exp, RMSE) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = exp, values_from = RMSE) %>%
  rename(Medina = `Medina et al.`, `Smith & Yu` = `Smith & Yu`,
         Suanda = `Suanda et al.`) %>%
  mutate(`Held-out mean` = (Medina + `Smith & Yu`) / 2) %>%
  arrange(`Held-out mean`) %>%
  mutate(Model = abbr_of(model), .before = 1) %>%
  select(Model, Medina, `Smith & Yu`, `Held-out mean`, Suanda)

gen_best <- gen_exps %>% group_by(exp) %>% slice_min(RMSE, n = 1) %>%
  select(exp, model, RMSE) %>% mutate(model = abbr_of(model))
best_of <- function(e) gen_best$model[gen_best$exp == e]
```


Using each model's group-fit parameters, we simulated its performance on further published experiments for which only group-level human accuracy is available.
@Medina2011 manipulated trial informativeness (the number of referents per trial) and the order of trials, over four between-subjects conditions with adults; @Smith2008vg and @yu2011you trained 12- and 14-month-old infants on 6 words across 30 trials, with infants learning about 4 words on average.
Neither experiment is in the fitting set, so both are genuine tests of generalization.
@Suanda2014, who varied contextual diversity for 6-year-olds, was held out in an earlier version of this comparison but has since been added to the fitting set; we report it here for continuity, with the caveat that the models were fit to it.
(@Koehne2013 was also held out in the earlier version and has likewise since been added to the fitting set, but we no longer break it out separately here -- its conditions are simply part of the 53-condition fit reported in Table 1.)
Table 3 gives the root-mean-square error (RMSE) between each model and average human performance on each experiment.

On the two genuinely held-out experiments, the models that generalize best are the simplest ones: the co-occurrence baseline, the Rescorla-Wagner and Kalman-filter models, and the reinforcement-learning model all predict the @Medina2011 trajectory and the @Smith2008vg data about as well as anything (RMSE near `r sprintf("%.2f", min(gen_wide$"Held-out mean"))`), while the more elaborate associative models -- the FU family and its variants -- fit these experiments worst.
In other words, the models generalize to held-out data roughly to the extent that they resemble co-occurrence counting.
The infant and child data (@Smith2008vg; @Suanda2014) are mostly underfit: the models tend to outperform the learners.
Among the now-in-set experiments, the @Suanda2014 data is best captured by the Bayesian decay model, as in the earlier comparison.

## Corpus Results

```{r corpus-results}
# From fits/corpus_results.R, which reshapes the XSLmodels package's own
# naturalistic-corpus comparison (tests/bakeoff_comparison/corpus_gold_*.R;
# see corpus_report.md there) -- not re-run here.
load(here("fits/corpus_results.RData"))

corpus_wide <- corpus_tab %>%
  filter(in_lab_roster | model %in% c("fgt2009", "fgt2009_rsa")) %>%
  mutate(Model = ifelse(is.na(lab_model), model, abbr_of(lab_model)),
         Model = case_when(model == "fgt2009" ~ "FGT",
                            model == "fgt2009_rsa" ~ "FGT-RSA",
                            TRUE ~ Model)) %>%
  select(Model, corpus, f_default, f_fitted) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = corpus, values_from = c(f_default, f_fitted),
              names_glue = "{corpus}_{.value}") %>%
  mutate(mean_fitted = rowMeans(select(., ends_with("f_fitted")), na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_fitted)) %>%
  select(Model, Rollins_f_default, Rollins_f_fitted, FM_f_default, FM_f_fitted, mean_fitted)
```

The models above were all fit to maximize agreement with human choices on short, curated laboratory experiments.
To ask whether the same mechanisms help recover word meanings from real caregiver speech, we ran every model (plus @Frank2009's batch Bayesian model, FGT, and its RSA-pragmatic extension, FGT-RSA) on the Rollins and FM corpora, scoring each model's learned matrix against the corpus's gold lexicon by best-threshold F.
We report two regimes: *default* parameters (each model's XSLmodels registry starting values, informed by the lab fits but not tuned to either corpus) and *corpus-fitted* parameters (re-optimized on each corpus to maximize gold-lexicon F).
Table 4 gives F for both regimes on both corpora, ordered by mean fitted F.

Fitting to the corpus helps every model, often substantially -- unsurprisingly, since registry defaults were tuned on short controlled experiments with none of a corpus's sparsity or non-referential noise.
The gain is largest for models whose defaults transfer worst: guess-and-test gains roughly .05-.06 F from fitting, and the item-level-prediction-error BAM variant (FU-P) gains .15-.32, while PA's defaults were already close to optimal for a corpus and barely move.
Two findings stand out for the comparison between laboratory and corpus performance (Spearman's $\rho$ = `r round(cor(rank_compare$lab_rank, rank_compare$corpus_rank, method="spearman"), 2)` between each model's lab rank and its corpus rank, computed over the `r nrow(rank_compare)` models tested in both settings): first, the Bayesian decay model -- middling in the lab comparison -- is the strongest model on *both* corpora, and FGT, the model purpose-built for exactly this inference problem, is close behind (its RSA extension makes almost no difference: the learned lexicon is too sparse for a heard word to ever name two co-present objects, so the pragmatic listener collapses to the literal one).
Second, the lab-best models diverge in how well they transfer: PA holds up as one of the strongest corpus models, while FUs -- the single best-fitting lab model -- falls to the middle of the corpus ranking, and the plain FU model it is built on fares only slightly better.
The hybrid Pursuit model, already the weakest lab fit, is also the weakest here, collapsing to a near-flat, uninformative matrix on the larger FM corpus.
<!-- ToDo (revision): re-check n_reversal / rank claims once the group fit is final. -->

```{r corpus-results-table, results="asis"}
ctab <- as.matrix(corpus_wide)
for (cc in c("Rollins_f_default", "Rollins_f_fitted", "FM_f_default", "FM_f_fitted")) {
  v <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(ctab[, cc]))
  ctab[, cc] <- ifelse(is.na(v), "--", sprintf("%.2f", v))
  if (any(!is.na(v))) {
    best_row <- which(v == max(v, na.rm = TRUE))
    ctab[best_row, cc] <- cell_spec(sprintf("%.2f", max(v, na.rm = TRUE)), "latex", bold = TRUE)
  }
}
ctab[, "mean_fitted"] <- sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(ctab[, "mean_fitted"]))
colnames(ctab) <- c("Model", "default", "fitted", "default", "fitted", "Mean fitted F")
kable(ctab, "latex", booktabs = T, escape = F,
      caption = "Best-threshold F recovering the gold lexicon on two naturalistic corpora, at registry-default and corpus-fitted parameters. FGT and FGT-RSA have no lab counterpart. Best per column in bold.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "scale_down") %>%
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Rollins" = 2, "FM" = 2, " " = 1))
```


# Discussion

We set out to conduct a systematic comparison of several models of cross-situational word learning models across a wide variety of experimental conditions. 
Using a large dataset, we found best-fitting parameters for 11 models both by simultaneously fitting all of the data, and using cross-validation.
The results of both fitting regimes were consistent and clear: shown in Table 1, the associative models generally achieved better fits (lower SSE and higher correlations) than the hypothesis-testing models (GnT; @Medina2011 and PbV; @Trueswell2013), which made correlated predictions (see Table 2: $r=.65$).
However, it was also striking how similar many models' predictions were, even to models representing disparate learning theories.

The Rescorla-Wagner model, a prediction error-based associative model, performed similarly to the GnT model, with highly correlated predictions ($r=.87$), while PbV had the poorest fit, and made responses most similar to the R-W model ($r=.67$).
Moreover, the predictions of the R-W model were also highly correlated with the baseline co-occurrence counting model ($r = .99$): such similar predictions yielded by seemingly different theories is surprising and warrants further investigation.
However, some models' particular patterns of responses suggest certain theoretical shortcomings.
For example, the hybrid Pursuit model [@Stevens2017pursuit] fared poorly, in part because it often outperformed humans ($M_{Pur} =$ `r round(mean(subset(gfd, Model=="pursuit")$ModelPerf), 2)`, $M_{hum} = 0.48$).
Indeed, as shown in Figure 1, Pur, PbV, and GnT all showed a pattern of inhuman responses: for a subset of items, the models either always got them correct or always got them incorrect, while people were more stochastic.
And yet Pur made responses that were most highly correlated with the FUs model ($r=.74$)--one of the best-fitting models.
In summary, although the hypothesis testing models evaluated here did not fare well, it is worth nothing that models from different theories can often mimic each other--at least in some experimental conditions--and so it is necessary to both 1) test other instances of general theories (including hypothesis testing models with, say, a decaying memory to reduce ceiling performance), and 2) use models to generate predictions during experiment design, in order to choose more informative experiments. 

<!-- There is even some suggestion that under certain assumptions models representing very different intuitions (e.g., storing a single hypothesized referent for each word vs. accumulating a word x referent association matrix representing all experienced co-occurrences) can mimic each other in some experimental conditions, making some model comparisons ill-posed altogether [@Yu2012hyp]. -->

Among the associative models, the PA model [@Fazly2010] and the FU model [@Kachergis2012gi] both fared quite well, and the sampling version of the FU model (FUs) performed slightly better, albeit with three free parameters compared to two in the PA model.
The predictions of the top three models were more correlated with each other than with the human data (see Table 1): PA vs. FUs: .87, PA vs. FU: .84, FU vs. FUs: .92.
But the PA model also showed a .84 correlation with the Rescorla-Wagner model, and both FU and FUs showed a .87 correlation with the simpler novelty-biased associative model (Nov)--stronger than for the uncertainty-bias mechanism used by the FU models.
Examining the experimental conditions that were easiest for the models to fit can indicate what types of designs are less useful to conduct to test theories of learning. 
For example, the condition best accounted for by six of the models had varied frequency (pairs appeared 3, 6, or 9 times) with low contextual diversity (i.e., the words of each frequency co-occurred only with each other): it turns out that showing a performance advantage for more frequent items is straightforward for many theories.
Future work should aim to further explore when these models make overlapping predictions, but another approach is to find conditions where models make disparate predictions. 
The FUs and PA models make maximally divergent predictions in the conditions with fewer words than objects per trial (esp. 1 word x 3 referents and 1 word x 4 referents conditions), which hints at a difference in mechanism for these models. 
A fruitful next step would be to use optimal experiment design to generate a definitive experiment to differentiate these models.
Models also struggled with conditions that tested how learners relax their bias for mutually exclusive pairings in the face of evidence that two words may both map to two referents: five models had the worst fit for conditions from @Kachergis2012gi.


Although we have aimed for broad coverage of models and experimental conditions, this study is far from complete in both respects.
First, there are many other models that we have not yet implemented [e.g., @mcmurray2012word]. <!-- or that we have not finished fitting to the data [e.g., @YurovskyFrank2015].  @tilles2012minimal; -->
Moreover, this dataset represents performance from a fairly homogeneous sample: English-speaking US college students. 
Future work should aim to include not only more models, but a more broadly diverse sample, both in terms of language background and age.
The small number of generalization experiments run here suggest that parameters fitted to adult experimental conditions do not generalize well to developmental experiments: future research should gather a larger set of developmental data and re-fit these models with cross-validation.
We invite other researchers to contribute datasets and model implementations for future, larger-scale comparisons: data, model code, and fitting procedures will be open-sourced and available on [OSF](https://osf.io/s2aty/?view_only=c91c852f00b847e0a71d5f4deaf7b7a5), as well as through an R package \texttt{XSLmodels} which we invite other to contribute to.

In summary, we have shown not only how a large model comparison can help rank models from most to least able to account for human data, but also how such comparisons can identify models that mimic each other, as well as identifying experimental designs that might aid in distinguishing models.
Future work should extend this comparison to cross-situational word learning models and extant datasets beyond those tested here, and design novel experiments designed to distinguish these models.
Finally, assuming that cross-situational learning is an important tool in the language learner's toolbelt, it is important to consider how these models can be extended to incorporate other information sources at the learner's disposal, such as social cues, pragmatics, and syntactic constraints on meaning [@HirshPasek2000; @Markman1990; @yurovsky2017beyond].
While many of these models have mechanisms for preferentially selecting and storing particular associations, most have yet to formally incorporate relevant cues from social partners--linguistic and nonlinguistic [though see @yurovsky2017beyond].
More broadly, we believe that structured model comparison is a critical step towards developing more complete models and, eventually, quantitative identification of the fundamental mechanisms of word learning.
